title: Volume Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: High School Geometry
description: Compare the volumes of two solids that share one width and one height, and discover the one-third relationship between pyramids and prisms and between cones and cylinders.

educational.topic: Volume formulas and volume relationships between solids
learningObjectives: Students will be able to apply volume formulas to prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres, and evaluate the volume relationships between related solids.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Controlled comparison: two solids constrained to share their dimensions
keyQuestions: Which pairs of solids have a constant ratio of volumes?
Why is the ratio 3 for a cylinder and its cone at every size?
What happens to a volume when the width doubles but the height stays fixed?
commonMisconceptions: A cone is half of a cylinder (it is one third).
Doubling the width doubles the volume (it multiplies the volume by four).
A sphere fills most of the cube that contains it (it fills about half).
assessmentOpportunities: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height, and the cylinder holds 540 cubic centimeters. Students state the cone's volume, then explain what happens to both volumes when the radius is doubled.
